question: A startup wants to avoid large upfront hardware purchases and pay only for the IT resources it actually uses. Which advantage of cloud computing does this describe?
options: Benefit from massive economies of scale
Trade fixed expense for variable expense
explanations: Agility is about how quickly resources can be made available, not how they are paid for.
Economies of scale explain why AWS prices are low, not how the startup pays.
Paying for resources as you consume them replaces upfront capital purchases.
Global reach is about deploying in many Regions quickly.
takeaway: Upfront purchases → variable, pay-as-you-go spending.

question: A retailer either buys too many servers for the holidays, which then sit idle, or too few, which causes outages. Which advantage of cloud computing addresses this problem?
options: Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
Benefit from massive economies of scale
explanations: Capacity can be added and removed as demand changes, so forecasts no longer have to be exact.
This is about facility costs, not matching capacity to demand.
Lower unit prices don’t remove the need to forecast capacity.
Deploying in more Regions doesn’t solve sizing for peak demand.
takeaway: Over- or under-provisioning → stop guessing capacity.

question: Which statement BEST describes how AWS customers benefit from economies of scale?
options: Customers share their servers with each other to split the cost
Each customer gets dedicated hardware at a discount for signing long contracts
AWS aggregates usage from many customers, which lowers its costs and prices
Prices are fixed for three years so budgets stay predictable
explanations: Customers don’t share servers with each other directly; AWS runs the infrastructure.
Shared infrastructure, not dedicated hardware, drives economies of scale.
Hundreds of thousands of customers share the infrastructure, so AWS can lower prices.
AWS prices aren’t fixed for set periods; many have fallen over time.
takeaway: Economies of scale = AWS’s size lowers costs for everyone.

question: A company based in Canada wants to serve customers in Japan with low latency without building a data center there. Which advantage of the AWS Cloud does this use?
options: Trade fixed expense for variable expense
explanations: Capacity planning isn’t the issue; location is.
The payment model doesn’t reduce latency for distant users.
The company can deploy in a Region near its users in minutes.
Agility is about quick provisioning in general, not geographic reach.
takeaway: Serve users in another part of the world quickly → go global in minutes.

question: A development team can now create a test environment in minutes and delete it when an experiment fails. Which benefit of the cloud does this demonstrate?
explanations: Availability is about keeping systems running, not experimenting quickly.
Elasticity adjusts capacity to load; this scenario is about experimenting quickly.
Economies of scale relate to lower prices, not experimentation.
Fast, low-cost provisioning makes it easy to try ideas and discard failures.
takeaway: Experiment quickly and cheaply → agility.

question: Traffic to a ticketing site grows tenfold for a few hours whenever concert tickets go on sale. Which cloud characteristic lets the site add resources for those hours and remove them automatically afterward?
explanations: Elastic systems scale out and in automatically as demand changes.
Agility is about how quickly you can experiment and deliver.
Durability is about not losing stored data.
Fault tolerance keeps a system running despite failures, not changes in load.
takeaway: Automatic scale out and in with demand → elasticity.

question: Which design MOST improves the availability of a web application running on Amazon EC2?
options: Run one larger instance with more CPU and memory
Store application data on instance store volumes
Run instances in multiple Availability Zones behind a load balancer
Place all instances in a single Availability Zone close to the database
explanations: A single instance is still a single point of failure.
Instance store data is lost when an instance stops, which reduces resilience.
If one AZ or instance fails, the load balancer sends traffic to healthy instances elsewhere.
One AZ is a single point of failure.
takeaway: High availability → multiple AZs + load balancing.

question: Which advantage of cloud computing lets a company focus on its customers instead of racking, stacking, and powering servers?
options: Benefit from massive economies of scale
Trade fixed expense for variable expense
Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
explanations: Economies of scale lower prices but aren’t about who operates the hardware.
Global reach is about deploying in many locations.
This is about the payment model, not the physical work.
AWS operates the facilities, so the company can focus on its business.
takeaway: No more racking and powering servers → stop spending on data centers.

question: Which TWO are benefits of moving workloads to the AWS Cloud? (Select TWO.)
options: AWS takes responsibility for securing customer data
Software licensing costs disappear for every application
Provisioning resources in minutes instead of weeks
Paying only for the resources that are used
Applications no longer need to be designed for failure
explanations: Customers remain responsible for their data under the shared responsibility model.
Many applications still need licenses.
On-demand provisioning speeds up delivery.
Pay-as-you-go pricing removes payment for idle capacity.
Cloud applications should still be designed for failure.
takeaway: Benefits: pay for what you use + fast provisioning.

question: A company must launch a new product in four weeks, but buying and installing servers in its data center takes three months. How does AWS help?
options: AWS Professional Services shorten the company’s purchasing approvals
Reserved Instances reserve physical hardware in the company’s data center
Resources can be provisioned on demand in minutes
AWS delivers servers to the company’s data center within days
explanations: Professional Services help with projects, not internal purchasing.
Reserved Instances are a pricing commitment for capacity in AWS Regions.
There is no hardware procurement cycle: resources are available immediately.
AWS doesn’t replace the company’s procurement with hardware deliveries for this need.
takeaway: Slow procurement → on-demand provisioning in minutes.

question: Which of the following is a pillar of the AWS Well-Architected Framework?
explanations: Scalability is a characteristic, not one of the six pillars.
Elasticity is a cloud benefit, not a pillar.
Agility is a cloud benefit, not a pillar.
Sustainability is the sixth pillar, alongside operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, and cost optimization.
takeaway: Six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability.

question: A company tests its recovery procedures regularly and designs its workloads to recover automatically from failures. Which Well-Architected pillar does this support?
explanations: Security protects data and systems.
Operational excellence covers running and improving operations.
Performance efficiency is about using resources efficiently.
Automatic recovery and tested recovery procedures are reliability design principles.
takeaway: Automatic recovery, tested recovery → reliability.

question: A team defines its infrastructure and operational procedures as code and makes frequent, small, reversible changes. Which Well-Architected pillar does this practice support?
explanations: Operations as code and small, reversible changes are operational excellence principles.
Cost optimization focuses on avoiding unnecessary costs.
Performance efficiency is about choosing efficient resources.
Reliability focuses on recovering from failures and meeting demand.
takeaway: Operations as code, small reversible changes → operational excellence.

question: Which design principle belongs to the security pillar of the Well-Architected Framework?
explanations: Logging and monitoring actions in real time is a security design principle.
This is a reliability design principle.
This is a cost optimization design principle.
This is a performance efficiency design principle.
takeaway: Traceability, strong identity, security at all layers → security pillar.

question: A company regularly evaluates new instance types and uses serverless architectures so that its workloads keep meeting demand efficiently. Which pillar does this support?
explanations: Cost optimization focuses on spending, not on matching resource types to performance needs.
Sustainability focuses on environmental impact.
Using the right resource types and serverless architectures are performance efficiency principles.
Reliability focuses on recovering from failure.
takeaway: Right resource types, serverless, experiment → performance efficiency.

question: Which practice aligns with the cost optimization pillar of the Well-Architected Framework?
options: Automating deployments with small, reversible changes
Deploying workloads across multiple Regions for disaster recovery
Analyzing spending by team with cost allocation tags
Encrypting all data at rest with AWS KMS
explanations: This supports operational excellence.
Multi-Region deployments support reliability and usually add cost.
Analyzing and attributing expenditure is a cost optimization principle.
Encryption supports the security pillar.
takeaway: Attribute and analyze spending → cost optimization.

question: Which action BEST supports the sustainability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework?
options: Maximizing utilization and removing idle resources
Choosing larger instance types to leave room for growth
Overprovisioning capacity to handle unexpected peaks
Keeping copies of all data in several Regions
explanations: High utilization reduces the energy needed per unit of work.
Oversized resources waste energy.
Idle capacity wastes energy.
Unneeded copies increase storage and energy use.
takeaway: Maximize utilization, remove waste → sustainability.

question: Which AWS service helps a team review a workload against AWS best practices by answering questions for each pillar of the Well-Architected Framework?
explanations: Config evaluates resource configurations against rules.
The tool walks through each pillar’s questions and creates an improvement plan.
The Health Dashboard shows AWS events that affect your resources.
Trusted Advisor runs automated account checks; it doesn’t guide a workload review.
takeaway: Question-based workload review → Well-Architected Tool.

question: Which TWO are design principles of the reliability pillar? (Select TWO.)
options: Scale horizontally to increase aggregate workload availability
explanations: Many small resources reduce the impact of a single failure.
Monitoring and automatic recovery are reliability principles.
This is a cost optimization principle.
This is a performance efficiency principle.
This is a security design principle.
takeaway: Reliability: recover automatically, test recovery, scale horizontally, stop guessing capacity.

question: A company’s goal is to reduce the carbon footprint of its workloads, not their cost. Which Well-Architected pillar gives the MOST relevant guidance?
explanations: Cost optimization focuses on spending; the goal here is environmental impact.
The sustainability pillar focuses on minimizing environmental impact.
Performance efficiency focuses on meeting requirements efficiently, not on environmental impact.
Reliability focuses on recovering from failure.
takeaway: Environmental impact → sustainability pillar.

question: Protecting data in transit and at rest is a design principle of which Well-Architected pillar?
explanations: Performance efficiency is about efficient use of resources.
Data protection in transit and at rest is a security design principle.
Operational excellence is about running and improving operations.
Reliability is about recovering from failure and meeting demand.
takeaway: Encryption in transit and at rest → security pillar.

question: A team uses runbooks, tracks operational metrics, and refines its procedures after every incident. Which Well-Architected pillar does this practice MOST directly support?
explanations: Performance efficiency focuses on efficient use of resources.
Learning from operational events and refining procedures are operational excellence principles.
Reliability focuses on the workload recovering from failures, not on improving team procedures.
Security focuses on protecting data and systems.
takeaway: Runbooks and post-incident learning → operational excellence.

question: Which AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) perspective focuses on staff skills, training, and organizational change for the cloud?
explanations: The business perspective connects cloud investments to business outcomes.
Governance focuses on managing risk, cost, and programs.
The people perspective covers culture, skills, training, and organizational structure.
The operations perspective focuses on running cloud services.
takeaway: Skills, training, culture → CAF people perspective.

question: Which AWS CAF perspective helps an organization manage cloud risk, costs, and program management?
explanations: Security focuses on protecting data and workloads.
Platform focuses on architecture and infrastructure.
Governance covers risk management, cloud financial management, and program management.
People focuses on skills and culture.
takeaway: Risk, cost, program management → CAF governance perspective.

question: Which AWS CAF perspective focuses on building a scalable cloud environment, including its architecture and infrastructure?
explanations: Governance focuses on risk and cost.
Operations focuses on running and monitoring services.
Business focuses on business outcomes and investments.
The platform perspective covers architecture, infrastructure, and engineering.
takeaway: Architecture and infrastructure → CAF platform perspective.

question: Which TWO are business outcomes that AWS CAF describes as benefits of cloud adoption? (Select TWO.)
options: Improved environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance
Removal of the need for IT governance
explanations: The cloud shifts spending away from capital expenses.
Customers remain responsible for their own compliance.
Reduced business risk is one of the four outcomes.
Improved ESG performance is one of the four outcomes.
Governance is still needed; it is one of the CAF perspectives.
takeaway: CAF outcomes: reduced risk, better ESG, more revenue, more operational efficiency.

question: A company wants to move its applications to AWS as quickly as possible without changing them. Which migration strategy should it use?
explanations: Rehosting (lift and shift) moves applications as they are.
Repurchasing replaces the application with a different product.
Refactoring re-architects the application, which takes longer.
Replatforming makes some cloud optimizations along the way.
takeaway: Move as is, quickly → rehost (lift and shift).

question: A company moves its self-managed MySQL database from its data center to Amazon RDS without changing the application code. Which migration strategy is this?
explanations: Moving to a managed service without changing the core application is replatforming (lift, tinker, and shift).
Refactoring would change the application’s architecture.
Rehosting would run the same self-managed database on EC2.
Relocate moves VMware-based workloads without changes.
takeaway: Lift, tinker, and shift (for example to RDS) → replatform.

question: A company replaces its self-hosted customer relationship management (CRM) system with a SaaS CRM product. Which migration strategy is this?
explanations: Retaining keeps the application where it is.
Replatforming keeps the same application with small optimizations.
Moving to a different product, often SaaS, is repurchasing.
Refactoring re-architects the existing application.
takeaway: Switch to a different (often SaaS) product → repurchase.

question: A company re-architects a monolithic application into microservices that use AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB to improve agility. Which migration strategy is this?
explanations: Re-architecting to use cloud-native features is refactoring.
Rehosting moves the application without changes.
Replatforming makes only small optimizations.
Relocating moves VMware workloads as they are.
takeaway: Re-architect for cloud-native features → refactor.

question: While planning a migration, a company finds several applications that nobody has used for a year. What is the MOST appropriate migration strategy for them?
explanations: Buying a replacement product isn’t needed for unused applications.
Retaining keeps them running, which still costs money.
Moving unused applications to AWS wastes effort and money.
Applications that are no longer needed should be switched off.
takeaway: Unused applications → retire.

question: A company doesn’t have the in-house expertise to plan and run a large data center migration. Which TWO options can provide hands-on help? (Select TWO.)
options: An AWS Partner such as a system integrator
explanations: Trusted Advisor gives automated best-practice checks, not hands-on migration help.
AWS Partners specialize in planning and running migrations.
Artifact provides compliance reports.
AWS experts can plan and deliver migrations with the customer’s team.
Inspector scans for vulnerabilities.
takeaway: Hands-on migration help → AWS Professional Services or AWS Partners.

question: A company must migrate a production database to AWS with minimal downtime. Which approach supports this requirement?
options: Export a full backup and restore it during a weekend outage
Copy the database files to Amazon S3 with the AWS CLI
Recreate the tables manually in Amazon RDS
Use AWS DMS to replicate changes continuously until cutover
explanations: This requires downtime while the backup is restored.
Copying files doesn’t keep the database in sync.
Manual recreation is slow and doesn’t move the data.
Continuous replication keeps the target in sync, so the final switch is quick.
takeaway: Minimal downtime → continuous replication with DMS.

question: A finance director wants a data-driven estimate of what the company’s current on-premises servers would cost to run on AWS before approving a migration. Which AWS offering helps build this business case?
explanations: DMS migrates databases.
Migration Evaluator analyzes current usage to project AWS costs and savings.
Migration Hub tracks migration progress.
This service performs rehost migrations; it doesn’t build a business case.
takeaway: Migration business case or TCO → Migration Evaluator.

question: Which cost is an example of a capital expense (CapEx) in an on-premises data center?
options: Buying servers and storage hardware up front
Paying per request for AWS Lambda
Paying monthly for the EC2 hours that were used
Paying per GB of data stored in Amazon S3
explanations: Upfront hardware purchases are capital expenses.
Per-request charges are variable operating expenses.
Usage-based charges are variable operating expenses.
Storage charges are variable operating expenses.
takeaway: Upfront hardware purchase → capital expense.

question: How does moving to AWS typically change a company’s IT cost structure?
options: Fixed upfront costs become variable costs that follow usage
Costs are billed once a year in advance
Variable costs become fixed monthly fees that are easier to forecast
explanations: Paying for resources as they are consumed replaces upfront purchases.
The cloud reduces capital expenses.
Most AWS charges are billed monthly based on usage.
The change goes the other way: fixed costs become variable.
takeaway: Fixed upfront costs → variable usage-based costs.

question: When comparing the total cost of ownership (TCO) of on-premises infrastructure with AWS, which TWO on-premises costs are often overlooked? (Select TWO.)
options: Fees for the AWS Basic Support plan
Power and cooling for the data center
Data transfer into AWS from the internet
Staff time to maintain and replace hardware
explanations: Basic Support is included at no cost.
Facility costs are part of on-premises TCO.
Free Tier usage isn’t an on-premises cost.
Inbound data transfer to AWS is free.
Labor for hardware maintenance and refreshes is a real on-premises cost.
takeaway: TCO includes facilities, power, cooling, and staff, not just servers.

question: A company owns Windows Server licenses that are counted per physical core. It wants to use these licenses on AWS. Which option supports this requirement?
options: On-Demand Instances with the license included
explanations: Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware but don’t show physical cores and sockets.
Spot Instances don’t give visibility of physical cores.
Dedicated Hosts give visibility of physical cores and sockets, which per-core licenses require.
License Included means paying for a new license, not bringing your own.
takeaway: Per-core or per-socket licenses (BYOL) → Dedicated Hosts.

question: A company wants to run Microsoft SQL Server on Amazon EC2 but doesn’t own any SQL Server licenses. Which licensing approach fits?
options: License Included instances, with the license cost in the hourly price
Bring your own license (BYOL) by running the instances on Dedicated Hosts
Generate new licenses with AWS License Manager
explanations: Artifact provides compliance reports, not software licenses.
AWS includes the license cost in the price of the instance.
BYOL requires licenses the company already owns.
License Manager tracks licenses; it doesn’t create them.
takeaway: No existing licenses → License Included pricing.

question: A company finds that many of its EC2 instances average 5% CPU utilization. Which cost optimization practice should it apply?
options: Deploying each instance in multiple Availability Zones
Scaling the instances vertically to larger sizes
explanations: Multi-AZ improves availability, not cost.
Moving to smaller or better-suited instance types removes paid but unused capacity.
Overprovisioning is the cause of the waste.
Larger instances would increase costs.
takeaway: Low utilization → rightsize.

question: How does using infrastructure as code help reduce operating costs?
options: It removes the need to pay for the resources in a template
It reduces the manual effort and errors of building and changing environments
It qualifies resources for Reserved Instance discounts automatically when they launch
It lowers the hourly price of the services it creates
explanations: Resources created from templates are still billed.
Automation replaces repetitive manual work and avoids costly mistakes.
Templates don’t affect pricing models.
Prices are the same however resources are created.
takeaway: Automation → less manual work, fewer errors.

question: A company runs a reporting job for two hours every night. Which characteristic of AWS pricing helps reduce the cost of this workload compared with dedicated on-premises servers?
options: Data processed inside an instance is free
Pay-as-you-go pricing charges only for the hours the job runs
AWS charges scheduled jobs a reduced fixed monthly fee for each server
Scheduled jobs must use reserved capacity
explanations: This doesn’t reduce compute cost.
Resources can run only during the job, so idle hours aren’t paid for.
Compute is charged for actual use, not a fixed monthly fee per server.
Reserved capacity isn’t required for scheduled jobs.
takeaway: Short scheduled jobs → pay only while they run.

question: Which AWS service helps a company track the software licenses it brings to AWS and prevent it from exceeding its license limits?
explanations: License Manager tracks license use and can enforce license rules.
Artifact provides compliance reports and agreements.
Marketplace sells third-party software.
Organizations manages accounts and policies.
takeaway: Track and enforce BYOL licenses → License Manager.

question: A company is comparing a $100,000 hardware purchase with running the same workload on AWS. Which approach gives the MOST accurate comparison?
options: Compare the hardware price with the AWS charges for the first month of running the workload
Compare total cost of ownership, including facilities, power, staff, and hardware refreshes
Compare the software license costs of both options side by side
Compare compute list prices after removing storage and networking
explanations: This ignores the useful life of the hardware and its running costs.
TCO captures all the costs of running on premises over time.
Licenses are just one part of the total cost.
Leaving out storage and networking makes the comparison incomplete.
takeaway: Fair comparison → total cost of ownership.

question: A company moves all of its servers out of a colocation data center to AWS. Which cost can it stop paying?
options: Rack space and power in the colocation facility
Staff who maintain the company’s application code
Licenses for the software its applications use
Data transfer out to its customers
explanations: AWS provides the facilities, so colocation fees end.
The company still owns and maintains its applications.
Software licenses may still be needed on AWS.
Data transfer out to the internet is still charged on AWS.
takeaway: Migrating removes facility costs, not application or license costs.

question: A company wants to reduce the time its staff spend on routine database tasks such as patching and backups. Which approach reduces this undifferentiated heavy lifting?
options: Move the databases to a managed service such as Amazon RDS
Hire more database administrators to provide around-the-clock support
Run the databases on Dedicated Hosts
Run the databases on larger EC2 instances
explanations: AWS handles patching, backups, and other routine tasks for RDS.
This adds cost instead of removing work.
Dedicated Hosts change the hardware tenancy, not who does maintenance.
The staff would still patch and back up the databases.
takeaway: Reduce undifferentiated heavy lifting → managed services.

question: A company says that moving to AWS lets it “fail fast” at low cost. Which characteristic of the cloud makes this possible?
options: Resources can be created for an experiment and deleted when they are no longer needed
Reserved Instances can be canceled without a fee when an experiment ends early
Test environments in AWS are free of charge
AWS refunds the cost of experiments that fail
explanations: There is no upfront investment, so failed experiments cost little.
Reserved Instances are a 1- or 3-year commitment.
Test resources are billed like any others.
AWS doesn’t refund usage for failed experiments.
takeaway: Experiment cheaply → create and delete resources on demand.

question: Which TWO factors reduce costs when a company moves from on-premises infrastructure to AWS? (Select TWO.)
options: Prices locked for the life of the account
Lower prices from AWS’s economies of scale
AWS manages application-level security for customers
No longer paying for idle capacity bought for peak demand
Free data transfer between AWS Regions
explanations: AWS prices aren’t locked for the life of an account.
AWS’s scale lowers its costs and prices.
Application security remains the customer’s responsibility.
Capacity can be matched to actual demand.
Data transfer between Regions is charged.
takeaway: Savings: no idle capacity + economies of scale.

question: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which task is AWS responsible for?
options: Physical security of the data centers
Configuring security groups for EC2 instances
Choosing encryption settings for customer data
explanations: AWS secures the facilities that run its services (security of the cloud).
Identity and access management is the customer’s responsibility.
Security group rules are configured by the customer.
Customers decide how their data is encrypted.
takeaway: Physical facilities and hardware → AWS.

question: Which task is the customer’s responsibility under the AWS shared responsibility model?
options: Maintaining the servers that run EC2 instances
Configuring IAM policies for its users
Securing the network between AWS data centers
explanations: AWS maintains the physical hosts.
The virtualization layer is AWS’s responsibility.
Customers control who can access their resources (security in the cloud).
AWS secures its global network infrastructure.
takeaway: IAM, data, and configuration → customer.

question: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. Who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
options: AWS, because EC2 is a managed service
AWS, when the instance was launched from an AWS-provided AMI
The publisher of the AMI, for as long as the instance runs
explanations: EC2 is infrastructure as a service; the guest OS belongs to the customer.
The AMI source doesn’t change responsibility after launch.
AMI publishers don’t patch running customer instances.
On EC2, the customer manages the guest OS, including patches.
takeaway: EC2 guest OS patching → customer.

question: A company uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Which task is AWS responsible for?
options: Deciding whether the database storage is encrypted
Configuring the security group that allows access to the database
Patching the database engine and the underlying operating system
Creating database users and granting their permissions
explanations: The customer chooses encryption settings.
Network access rules are the customer’s responsibility.
For managed databases, AWS patches the OS and database software.
Database users and permissions are managed by the customer.
takeaway: RDS: AWS patches OS and engine; customer manages access and data.

question: Which task remains the customer’s responsibility when using AWS Lambda?
options: Managing the function code and its IAM permissions
Maintaining the infrastructure behind the runtime
Patching the operating system that runs the functions
Adding servers when the number of requests grows
explanations: Customers own their code, its permissions, and their data.
AWS maintains the infrastructure and runtimes.
AWS manages the servers and operating systems for Lambda.
Lambda scales automatically.
takeaway: Lambda: customer owns code, permissions, and data.

question: Which TWO are customer responsibilities when using Amazon EC2? (Select TWO.)
options: Controlling physical access to the data center
Replacing failed physical disks in the host
explanations: The virtualization layer is AWS’s responsibility.
Physical security is AWS’s responsibility.
AWS maintains the physical hardware.
The customer manages the OS on its instances.
The customer controls network access to its instances.
takeaway: EC2: guest OS, applications, security groups, data → customer.

question: A company moves a workload from Amazon EC2 to Amazon RDS and later to AWS Lambda. How does its share of security responsibility change?
options: It decreases, because AWS manages more of the underlying stack
It stays the same, because responsibility depends on the data stored, not the service
AWS takes over code and data security once the workload is serverless
It increases, because each service adds settings to configure
explanations: With managed and serverless services, AWS takes over OS and infrastructure tasks.
Responsibility also depends on the type of service.
Customers still own their code, data, and permissions.
More managed services remove tasks from the customer.
takeaway: More managed service → less customer responsibility (but never none).

question: Which of the following is a shared control between AWS and the customer?
options: Logging access to AWS data centers
explanations: Data center access is controlled by AWS.
These are AWS’s responsibility.
AWS patches the infrastructure; customers patch their guest OS and applications.
Data classification is the customer’s responsibility.
takeaway: Shared controls: patch management, configuration management, awareness and training.

question: A company must encrypt the objects in its Amazon S3 bucket with its own customer managed AWS KMS key. Who is responsible for configuring this?
options: Both, with AWS creating and assigning the key automatically
AWS, as part of S3 default encryption
AWS, after the company opens a support case
explanations: Choosing and configuring encryption with its own key is the customer’s responsibility.
The customer creates and selects its customer managed key.
Default encryption uses S3-managed keys unless the customer chooses otherwise.
Customers configure encryption themselves.
takeaway: Encryption choices and key management settings → customer.

question: Which is AWS’s responsibility for Amazon S3?
options: Keeping the underlying storage infrastructure durable and available
Deciding which users can read objects
explanations: AWS runs and maintains the storage infrastructure.
Bucket policies are written by the customer.
Versioning is a setting the customer chooses.
Access decisions are the customer’s.
takeaway: S3 infrastructure → AWS. Access and settings → customer.

question: A company stores data in Amazon DynamoDB. Which task is the customer’s responsibility?
options: Controlling access to the tables with IAM
Replicating table data across Availability Zones
Providing redundant power for the storage nodes
Patching the servers that run DynamoDB
explanations: Customers decide who can access their data.
DynamoDB replicates data automatically.
AWS manages the infrastructure.
AWS manages the servers.
takeaway: Serverless database: customer controls access and data.

question: Which statement about the AWS shared responsibility model is correct?
options: AWS secures customer data once it is uploaded to an AWS service
Responsibilities are written separately into each customer’s contract
Customers secure the physical hosts that run their instances
AWS is responsible for security of the cloud, and customers for security in the cloud
explanations: Customers remain responsible for their data.
The model applies to all customers in the same way.
Physical hosts are AWS’s responsibility.
This is the core of the shared responsibility model.
takeaway: Security OF the cloud → AWS. Security IN the cloud → customer.

question: Where can a company download AWS SOC and ISO compliance reports?
explanations: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities.
Config evaluates resource configurations.
Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations.
Artifact provides on-demand access to AWS compliance reports.
takeaway: AWS compliance reports → AWS Artifact.

question: A healthcare company must review and accept the AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA). Which service should it use?
explanations: Service Catalog shares approved products.
Organizations manages accounts and policies.
Artifact lets customers review and accept agreements such as the BAA.
Support Center is for support cases.
takeaway: Agreements such as the BAA → AWS Artifact.

question: Which statement about compliance on AWS is correct?
options: Workloads on AWS automatically inherit full regulatory compliance
AWS certifications also cover the customer’s own applications
Customers must audit AWS data centers themselves
AWS infrastructure is certified, but customers must make their own workloads compliant
explanations: Customers must configure their own workloads to be compliant.
Certifications cover AWS infrastructure, not customer applications.
Third-party auditors assess AWS; customers use their reports.
Customers inherit infrastructure controls and remain responsible for their own configurations.
takeaway: AWS compliance covers the infrastructure; your workload’s compliance is yours.

question: A company must keep customer data within Germany to meet a data residency law. What should it do?
options: Store and process the data in an AWS Region located in Germany
Ask AWS Support to keep the data inside Germany
Cache the data in Germany with Amazon CloudFront
Encrypt the data with AWS KMS in any Region
explanations: Customers choose the Region, and AWS doesn’t move data out of it.
Customers control data location by choosing the Region.

Config records configurations, not every API call.

question: Which IAM feature produces a report that lists all users and the status of their passwords, access keys, and MFA devices?

The credential report lists every user and the status of their credentials.

question: What does the principle of least privilege mean?

Share one set of credentials across the whole team
Give administrators full access and restrict everyone else
Use the root user for daily administration
explanations: Minimal permissions limit damage from mistakes or stolen credentials.
Shared credentials prevent accountability.
Administrators should also have only what they need.
The root user shouldn’t be used for daily work.
takeaway: Least privilege = only the permissions needed.

Create access keys for the root user to automate tasks
Share the root password with the operations team
Use the root user to create all new resources

Root access keys are a major risk and shouldn’t exist.
Sharing the root password removes accountability.
Daily work should use IAM Identity Center or IAM identities.

question: Which task can be performed only by the AWS account root user?
options: Creating a billing alarm in CloudWatch
explanations: Identities with permission can create alarms.
Administrators can create IAM users.
Closing the account requires the root user.
Any identity with permission can launch instances.

question: An application running on Amazon EC2 needs to read objects from an S3 bucket. What is the MOST secure way to grant access?

Attach an IAM role to the instance with read access to the bucket
Store an IAM user’s access keys in the application code
Use the root user’s access keys

Roles give temporary credentials that rotate automatically.
Keys in code can leak and don’t rotate automatically.
Root keys give unlimited access and shouldn’t exist.
takeaway: Applications on AWS → IAM roles.

question: Ten developers need the same set of permissions. What is the simplest way to manage them?

Create a separate IAM role for each developer

Per-person roles add work without benefit here.

Customer managed policies are created by the customer.
SCPs are created by customers in AWS Organizations.

explanations: Separate users in each account means many credentials.

IAM users are for people and apps that work with your AWS account.
Cognito provides sign-up and sign-in, including social identity providers.

A password policy sets rules for passwords only.

An account password policy in IAM

Secrets Manager rotates application secrets, not user passwords.

IAM users with access keys in each account

takeaway: Access across accounts without new credentials → cross-account roles.

S3 doesn’t rotate credentials.

Access keys are long-term until they are rotated or deleted.
Console sign-in uses a password, not access keys.
Access keys are long-term credentials for the CLI, SDKs, and APIs.

explanations: Dedicated Hosts change tenancy, not who manages the database.
On EC2 the company patches, backs up, and scales the database.
RDS handles patching, backups, and recovery.
Outposts doesn’t remove database administration.
takeaway: Relational database, least overhead → RDS or Aurora.

question: When might a company choose to run a database on Amazon EC2 instead of Amazon RDS?
options: When it wants the least operational overhead
When it wants AWS to handle patching and backups
When it needs automatic Multi-AZ failover
When it needs OS access or a database engine that RDS doesn’t support
explanations: RDS has less overhead than EC2.
That is a reason to choose RDS.
RDS Multi-AZ provides this.
EC2 gives full control for unsupported engines or OS-level needs.
takeaway: Need OS access or an unsupported engine → database on EC2.

question: A social network needs to store and query relationships between users, such as friends of friends. Which database service is designed for this?
explanations: DynamoDB is a key-value database; relationship queries are not its strength.
Relational databases struggle with deep relationship queries.
DocumentDB stores JSON documents.
Neptune is a graph database for highly connected data.
takeaway: Relationships between entities → Neptune.

question: Which Amazon RDS feature keeps a synchronous standby copy of a database in another Availability Zone for automatic failover?
explanations: Read replicas are asynchronous and serve read traffic.
Snapshots are point-in-time copies.
Backups allow restores, not automatic failover.
Multi-AZ replicates synchronously to a standby and fails over automatically.
takeaway: Standby + automatic failover → RDS Multi-AZ.

question: A company is migrating an Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. Which TWO AWS services should it use? (Select TWO.)
explanations: DMS moves the data and replicates ongoing changes.
Migration Evaluator builds a business case.
This service rehosts servers, not databases between engines.
SCT converts the Oracle schema and code to PostgreSQL.
Backup protects data; it doesn’t migrate between engines.
takeaway: Different engines → SCT (schema) + DMS (data).

question: A company wants to move a MongoDB workload to a managed AWS database with minimal application changes. Which service should it choose?
explanations: DynamoDB uses its own APIs, so the application would need changes.
Aurora is relational.
Neptune is a graph database.
DocumentDB is compatible with MongoDB APIs and drivers.
takeaway: MongoDB compatibility → DocumentDB.

question: Which AWS service lets a company create a logically isolated virtual network?
explanations: A VPC is your own isolated network in AWS.
CloudFront is a content delivery network.
Direct Connect links your premises to AWS.
Route 53 is a DNS service.
takeaway: Isolated virtual network → Amazon VPC.

question: Which VPC component allows resources in a public subnet to communicate with the internet?
explanations: A NAT gateway gives private subnets outbound-only access.
A virtual private gateway terminates VPN connections.
An internet gateway connects the VPC to the internet.
Transit Gateway connects VPCs and networks.
takeaway: Public subnet internet access → internet gateway.

question: Instances in a private subnet must download software updates from the internet but must not accept inbound connections from the internet. What should the company use?
options: An internet gateway attached to the private subnet
A security group that allows all inbound traffic
explanations: Routing to an internet gateway would make the subnet public.
This would expose the instances.
A NAT gateway allows outbound connections only.
Peering connects VPCs, not the internet.
takeaway: Outbound-only internet for private subnets → NAT gateway.

question: Which statement about security groups is correct?
options: They are stateless and support deny rules
They require rules that allow return traffic explicitly
They are stateful and support allow rules only
They are applied at the subnet level
explanations: That describes network ACLs.
Return traffic is allowed automatically.
Security groups track connections and only allow traffic.
Security groups apply to instances and other resources.
takeaway: Security groups: stateful, allow-only, resource level.

question: A company needs to block traffic from a specific IP address range to every instance in a subnet. What should it use?
options: An IAM policy that denies the IP range
A security group with a deny rule
A route table entry for the IP range
A network ACL with a deny rule
explanations: IAM controls API access, not network traffic to instances.
Security groups can’t deny traffic.
Route tables direct traffic; they don’t filter it.
Network ACLs filter traffic at the subnet level and support deny rules.
takeaway: Deny an IP range for a subnet → network ACL.

question: Which AWS service provides DNS and domain name registration?
explanations: Route 53 is AWS’s DNS and domain registration service.
API Gateway manages APIs.
CloudFront delivers content.
VPC provides private networks.
takeaway: DNS and domains → Route 53.

question: A company needs a dedicated, private connection from its data center to AWS with consistent network performance. Which service should it use?
explanations: Direct Connect provides a dedicated private link with consistent performance.
Client VPN connects individual users.
A VPN runs over the internet, so performance can vary.
Global Accelerator speeds up user traffic to applications.
takeaway: Dedicated, consistent connection → Direct Connect.

question: A company needs to connect its office network to a VPC securely today, over the internet, at low cost. Which option should it choose?
explanations: CloudFront delivers content to users.
Direct Connect takes weeks to provision and costs more.
A Site-to-Site VPN can be set up quickly and encrypts traffic over the internet.
Transit Gateway is a hub; it still needs a VPN or Direct Connect to reach the office.
takeaway: Fast, low-cost encrypted link → Site-to-Site VPN.

question: Remote employees need secure access to internal applications in a VPC from their laptops. Which service should the company use?
explanations: Client VPN gives individual users encrypted access.
Site-to-Site VPN connects networks, not individual devices.
Direct Connect links a data center, not laptops.
Peering connects VPCs.
takeaway: Individual remote users → Client VPN.

question: Which option lets resources in a VPC reach supported AWS services privately, without an internet gateway or NAT gateway?
explanations: Transit Gateway connects networks; it doesn’t provide private service endpoints.
Interface endpoints keep traffic to AWS services on the AWS network.
Route 53 resolves names; it doesn’t change the network path.
Global Accelerator improves internet traffic to applications.
takeaway: Private access to AWS services from a VPC → PrivateLink endpoints.

question: Which AWS service provides object storage?
explanations: S3 stores objects in buckets.
EFS provides file storage.
EBS provides block storage.
Storage Gateway connects on-premises apps to cloud storage.
takeaway: Object storage → S3.

question: Which storage option provides persistent block storage for an EC2 instance?
explanations: EFS is a shared file system.
Instance store is block storage, but its data is lost when the instance stops.
EBS volumes persist independently of the instance.
S3 is object storage.
takeaway: Persistent block storage → EBS.

question: A fleet of Linux web servers needs to read and write the same files at the same time. Which service should the company use?
explanations: EFS is a shared file system that many instances can mount.
Glacier classes are for archives.
Instance store is local to one instance and temporary.
An EBS volume is attached to a single instance in most cases.
takeaway: Shared Linux file system → EFS.

question: A company needs Windows file shares that use the SMB protocol and integrate with Active Directory. Which service should it use?
options: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
explanations: FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB shares with Active Directory integration.
EBS is block storage for single instances.
S3 is object storage, not SMB file shares.
EFS provides NFS for Linux.
takeaway: Windows SMB shares → FSx for Windows File Server.

question: Data in an S3 bucket has unknown and changing access patterns. Which storage class lowers cost without performance impact or operational overhead?
explanations: Standard is priced for frequently accessed data.
Deep Archive retrievals take hours.
One Zone-IA charges retrieval fees and keeps data in one AZ.
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically.
takeaway: Unknown access patterns → S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

question: A company must keep financial records for 10 years. The records are almost never accessed, and a retrieval time of 12 hours is acceptable. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective?
explanations: Standard-IA is for data that needs immediate access.
Deep Archive is the lowest-cost class, with retrievals in hours.
Instant Retrieval costs more because it returns data in milliseconds.
Intelligent-Tiering suits unknown patterns; this pattern is known.
takeaway: Rarely accessed archive, hours are fine → Glacier Deep Archive.

question: A company wants objects to move automatically from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval 90 days after they are created. What should it configure?
explanations: Replication copies objects to another bucket.
Versioning keeps object versions; it doesn’t move objects between classes.
Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads over long distances.
Lifecycle rules transition objects between storage classes on a schedule.
takeaway: Move or expire objects over time → S3 Lifecycle.

question: An application needs temporary storage for cache and scratch data with very high I/O performance, and losing the data when the instance stops is acceptable. Which storage is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes
explanations: Provisioned IOPS volumes are persistent and cost extra.
EFS is shared network storage, not the fastest local scratch space.
S3 isn’t block storage for scratch data.
Instance store is fast local storage included in the instance price, but it is temporary.
takeaway: Fast, temporary scratch storage → instance store.

question: An on-premises application needs to store files in Amazon S3 while keeping a local cache of recently used files. Which service should the company use?
explanations: EFS is a cloud file system for AWS compute.
File Gateway presents S3 as a file share with a local cache.
Direct Connect provides a network link, not storage.
Backup manages backups, not file access with a cache.
takeaway: On-premises access to cloud storage with a local cache → Storage Gateway.

question: A company wants to manage backup schedules and retention for EBS volumes, RDS databases, and DynamoDB tables from one place. Which service should it use?
explanations: Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers for failover.
AWS Backup manages policy-based backups across many services.
Storage Gateway provides hybrid storage access.
Snapshots cover EBS only.
takeaway: Centralized backups across services → AWS Backup.

question: Which AWS service converts text into lifelike speech?
explanations: Transcribe converts speech to text.
Polly turns text into speech.
Comprehend analyzes text.
Translate converts text between languages.
takeaway: Text → speech: Polly.

question: Which AWS service extracts printed text, forms, and tables from scanned documents?
explanations: Rekognition analyzes images and video.
Comprehend analyzes text that is already digital.
Textract extracts text and structured data from documents.
Translate translates text.
takeaway: Text and data from documents → Textract.

question: A company wants to analyze customer reviews to find out whether they are positive or negative. Which service should it use?
explanations: Polly converts text to speech.
Lex builds chatbots.
Rekognition analyzes images and video.
Comprehend detects sentiment and other insights in text.
takeaway: Sentiment in text → Comprehend.

question: A company wants to build a chatbot that understands customer requests written in natural language. Which service should it use?
explanations: Textract extracts data from documents.
Polly converts text to speech.
Transcribe converts speech to text.
Lex builds conversational interfaces that recognize intents.
takeaway: Chatbot → Lex.

question: Data scientists want to build, train, and deploy their own machine learning models on managed infrastructure. Which service should they use?
explanations: SageMaker AI provides tools to build, train, and deploy custom models.
Rekognition offers pre-trained vision models.
Amazon Q is a generative AI assistant.
Comprehend offers pre-trained language models.
takeaway: Build and train your own models → SageMaker AI.

question: Analysts want to run SQL queries directly on log files stored in Amazon S3 without loading them into a database or managing servers. Which service should they use?
explanations: Redshift is a data warehouse that usually loads data first.
EMR runs big data clusters that need managing.
Glue prepares and catalogs data; it isn’t the query tool.
Athena runs serverless SQL queries on data in S3.
takeaway: Serverless SQL on S3 → Athena.

question: A company needs to collect and process clickstream data from its website in real time. Which service should it use?
explanations: Glue runs ETL jobs on data at rest.
Athena queries data at rest in S3.
Redshift analyzes stored historical data.
Kinesis ingests and processes streaming data in real time.
takeaway: Real-time streaming data → Kinesis.

question: Which service creates interactive business intelligence dashboards from data in sources such as Amazon Redshift?
explanations: Glue prepares data.
Quick Sight builds BI dashboards and visualizations.
Kinesis ingests streaming data.
Athena runs SQL queries.
takeaway: BI dashboards → Quick Sight.

question: A company wants to decouple its order system so that orders are held until worker instances are ready to process them. Which service should it use?
explanations: SNS pushes messages to subscribers immediately; it doesn’t hold them for workers.
SQS stores messages in a queue until consumers process them.
SES sends email.
Step Functions orchestrates workflows.
takeaway: Buffer work between components → SQS.

question: A company wants to send a message to many subscribers, including email addresses and Lambda functions, whenever an event happens. Which service should it use?
explanations: Kinesis handles streaming data.
SQS queues messages for consumers to pull.
SES sends email but doesn’t deliver to Lambda subscribers.
SNS publishes a message to every subscriber of a topic.
takeaway: One message to many subscribers → SNS.

question: A company wants to set up a cloud-based contact center for customer service calls. Which service should it use?
explanations: SNS sends notifications.
SES sends email.
Lex builds chatbots, which can be used inside a contact center.
Connect provides a cloud contact center with phone and chat.
takeaway: Contact center → Amazon Connect.

question: Which service gives employees persistent virtual desktops that they can access from almost any device?
explanations: WorkSpaces provides managed virtual desktops.
Secure Browser provides access to web applications only.
Lightsail provides simple servers, not end-user desktops.
AppStream 2.0 streams individual applications.
takeaway: Virtual desktops → WorkSpaces.

question: Which service traces requests through a distributed application to help developers find performance bottlenecks?
explanations: X-Ray traces requests across services.
CloudTrail records API calls to AWS.
CodePipeline automates releases.
Inspector scans for vulnerabilities.
takeaway: Trace requests and find bottlenecks → X-Ray.

question: A company needs to connect thousands of sensors securely and route their data to other AWS services. Which service should it use?
explanations: IoT Core connects devices and routes their messages with rules.
SQS queues messages between application components.
API Gateway manages APIs, not device connections.
Amplify builds web and mobile apps.
takeaway: Connect and manage IoT devices → IoT Core.

question: Which EC2 purchasing option is BEST for a short-term workload with unpredictable usage that must not be interrupted?
explanations: Dedicated Hosts are for licensing or compliance needs.
Reserved Instances need a 1- or 3-year commitment.
Spot Instances can be interrupted.
On-Demand has no commitment and isn’t interrupted.
takeaway: Short-term, unpredictable, uninterruptible → On-Demand.

question: A company runs a database server 24 hours a day and plans to keep it for three years. Which purchasing option gives the LARGEST discount?
options: A 3-year Standard Reserved Instance paid All Upfront
A 1-year Convertible Reserved Instance with No Upfront payment
explanations: Spot Instances can be interrupted, which a database can’t tolerate.
The longest term, Standard type, and full upfront payment give the biggest discount.
A shorter term, Convertible type, and no upfront payment give a smaller discount.
On-Demand has the highest price.
takeaway: Steady usage: longer term + more upfront = bigger discount.

question: Which workload is the BEST fit for EC2 Spot Instances?
options: A licensed application tied to a physical server
A production database that must stay online
A checkout service with steady traffic around the clock
Batch image processing that can restart if it is interrupted
explanations: This needs Dedicated Hosts.
Interruptions would take the database offline.
Steady, critical workloads fit Reserved Instances or Savings Plans.
Spot suits flexible, fault-tolerant work.
takeaway: Interruptible, flexible work → Spot.

question: A company wants to commit to a consistent amount of compute spend for one year and have the discount apply automatically across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda. Which option should it choose?
explanations: EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply to one instance family in one Region.
Reserved Instances apply only to matching EC2 usage.
Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda.
Spot isn’t a commitment-based discount.
takeaway: Flexible commitment across EC2, Fargate, Lambda → Compute Savings Plans.

question: What is the main difference between Standard and Convertible Reserved Instances?
options: Standard Reserved Instances don’t require a term commitment
Convertible Reserved Instances also cover Lambda and Fargate
Standard Reserved Instances can be canceled at any time
Convertible RIs can be exchanged for other instance families, for a smaller discount
explanations: Both types require a 1- or 3-year term.
That describes Compute Savings Plans.
Both types are a commitment for the full term.
Flexibility to change attributes costs some of the discount.
takeaway: Convertible = more flexibility, smaller discount.

question: A company must make sure EC2 capacity is available in a specific Availability Zone for a product launch next week, without a long-term commitment. Which option should it use?
explanations: Spot capacity isn’t guaranteed.
Dedicated Instances change tenancy, not capacity guarantees.
Savings Plans give discounts but don’t reserve capacity.
Capacity Reservations guarantee capacity in an AZ for any duration.
takeaway: Guarantee capacity in an AZ, no long commitment → Capacity Reservations.

question: A company uses AWS Organizations with consolidated billing. One account bought Reserved Instances that it no longer fully uses, and another account runs matching instances. What happens?
options: The other account must buy its own Reserved Instances to get a discount
The unused Reserved Instances are refunded at the end of the month
The unused Reserved Instance discount can apply to the matching usage in the other account
The Reserved Instances move permanently to the account with the most usage
explanations: Discount sharing lets it benefit without buying.
Reserved Instances aren’t refunded.
RI discounts are shared across accounts in the organization by default.
Ownership doesn’t change; the discount is applied on the bill.
takeaway: Consolidated billing shares RI and Savings Plans discounts.

question: Which type of data transfer is generally free of charge?
options: Data transferred into AWS from the internet
Data transferred out of Amazon S3 to the internet
Data transferred out from EC2 to the internet
explanations: Inbound data transfer is free.
Inter-Region transfer is charged.
Data transfer out to the internet is charged.
Data transfer out to the internet is charged.
takeaway: Inbound → free. Outbound and between Regions → charged.

question: Compliance rules require a company’s instances to run on hardware that no other AWS customer uses. The company doesn’t need visibility of physical cores or sockets. Which option is the MOST cost-effective?
explanations: Dedicated Hosts give a whole server and core visibility, which costs more than needed here.
Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware without paying for a whole host.
Spot runs on shared hardware and can be interrupted.
Shared tenancy doesn’t meet the requirement.
takeaway: Single-tenant hardware without core visibility → Dedicated Instances.

question: Which TWO factors affect what a company pays for Amazon S3? (Select TWO.)
options: Data transferred out of S3 to the internet
The AWS Region where the account was created
The number of IAM users who can access the bucket
The storage class and the amount of data stored
Data uploaded into S3 from the internet
explanations: Data transfer out is charged per GB.
Account creation location doesn’t affect pricing.
IAM users don’t affect S3 charges.
Storage is priced per GB and varies by class.
Inbound data transfer is free.
takeaway: S3 cost: storage (by class) + requests + retrieval + data transfer out.

question: Which AWS tool estimates the monthly cost of an architecture before it is deployed?
explanations: The Pricing Calculator models the cost of planned resources.
Budgets alerts on spending against a limit.
Cost Explorer analyzes costs that have already happened.
Cost and Usage Reports provide detailed historical billing data.
takeaway: Estimate before building → Pricing Calculator.

question: Which service sends an alert when actual or forecasted costs exceed an amount that the company sets?
explanations: Cost Explorer visualizes and forecasts costs but doesn’t send threshold alerts.
These reports provide detailed data, not alerts.
The Pricing Calculator estimates costs before deployment.
Budgets notifies you when spend crosses a threshold.
takeaway: Alert on spending thresholds → AWS Budgets.

question: A manager wants to see which services caused last month’s increase in AWS spending and view a forecast for next month. Which tool should the manager use?
explanations: Cost Explorer shows costs by service over time and forecasts future spend.
The Pricing Calculator estimates planned costs.
Budgets tracks spending against limits.
Trusted Advisor recommends savings but doesn’t analyze trends.
takeaway: Analyze past spend and forecast → Cost Explorer.

question: A company wants to track its AWS costs by department. What should it do?
options: Turn on AWS Config in each department’s resources
Create a separate IAM user for each department
Tag resources with a department tag and activate it as a cost allocation tag
Use the Pricing Calculator for each department
explanations: Config tracks configurations, not costs.
IAM users don’t organize costs.
Activated tags let you group costs by department.
The calculator estimates costs; it doesn’t track actual spend.
takeaway: Costs by department or project → cost allocation tags.

question: Which AWS billing feature provides the most detailed, line-item cost and usage data that can be analyzed with Amazon Athena?
explanations: Cost Explorer shows summarized views, not every line item.
Budgets tracks spending against limits.
The dashboard summarizes charges.
Cost and Usage Reports deliver line-item data to S3 for analysis.
takeaway: Most granular billing data → Cost and Usage Reports.

question: Which TWO are benefits of consolidated billing in AWS Organizations? (Select TWO.)
options: Free AWS Support for member accounts
Automatic Reserved Instance purchases for steady workloads
One bill for all accounts in the organization
Combined usage that reaches volume pricing discounts sooner
explanations: Billing doesn’t delete resources.
Support plans are still charged.
Consolidated billing shares discounts but never buys commitments for you.
The management account pays for all member accounts.
Usage is aggregated across accounts for tiered pricing.
takeaway: Consolidated billing: one bill + volume discounts + shared RIs/Savings Plans.

question: Where can a company see its current bill, its invoices, and the credits applied to its account?
options: The AWS Billing and Cost Management console
explanations: The Health Dashboard shows service events.
The billing console shows bills, invoices, payments, and credits.
Trusted Advisor provides recommendations.
Artifact provides compliance reports and agreements.
takeaway: Bills, invoices, credits → Billing and Cost Management console.

question: Which AWS Support plan includes a designated technical account manager (TAM)?
explanations: Enterprise Support includes a designated TAM.
Professional Services is a consulting offering, not a support plan.
Business Support+ gives 24/7 support engineers but no designated TAM.
Basic Support includes account and billing help only.
takeaway: Designated TAM → Enterprise Support (or Unified Operations).

question: Which of the following is included with AWS Basic Support at no cost?
options: Technical support cases with a 30-minute response
The full set of Trusted Advisor checks
Customer service for account and billing questions
explanations: Technical cases need a paid plan.
Basic includes only the core checks.
A TAM comes with Enterprise Support.
Basic Support includes 24/7 customer service for account and billing.
takeaway: Basic: account and billing help, docs, re:Post, Health Dashboard, core checks.

question: A startup with production workloads needs 24/7 access to AWS technical support and the full set of Trusted Advisor checks at the lowest cost. Which plan should it choose?
explanations: Business Support+ is the lowest-cost plan with 24/7 technical support and all checks.
Unified Operations is the most expensive plan.
Basic doesn’t include technical support.
Enterprise meets the needs but costs much more.
takeaway: Cheapest 24/7 technical support → Business Support+.

question: A company receives spam emails that seem to come from an Amazon EC2 instance. Whom should it contact?
options: AWS Support, by opening a technical case
explanations: Trust & Safety handles reports of abuse from AWS resources.
Professional Services helps customers build and migrate.
Partners help customers with projects.
Support cases are for your own account’s issues.
takeaway: Abuse from AWS resources → AWS Trust & Safety.

question: Which AWS resource is a community-driven Q&A site where users ask and answer technical questions about AWS?
explanations: Artifact provides compliance reports.
Marketplace sells third-party software.
re:Post is AWS’s community Q&A service.
Trusted Advisor gives automated recommendations.
takeaway: Community Q&A → AWS re:Post.

question: A company wants a consulting firm with AWS expertise to help migrate and modernize its applications. Where should it look?
options: The AWS Partner Network, for a system integrator or consulting partner
explanations: Trusted Advisor gives automated recommendations.
AWS Partners include consulting firms and system integrators.
re:Post is a community Q&A site.
Artifact provides compliance documents.
takeaway: Consulting help → AWS Partners (or AWS Professional Services).

question: Which service gives a company notifications about AWS scheduled maintenance that will affect its EC2 instances?
explanations: Trusted Advisor checks best practices.
The Health Dashboard shows events, including scheduled maintenance, that affect your resources.
Config records configuration changes.
CloudTrail records API activity.
takeaway: AWS events affecting your resources → AWS Health Dashboard.
